claim: Fast synaptic inhibition in the nervous system depends on the transmembrane flux of Cl- ions based on the neuronal Cl- driving force.
source: Fast synaptic inhibition in the nervous system depends on the transmembrane flux of Cl- ions based on the neuronal Cl- driving force.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that establishes the fundamental relationship between chloride flux and synaptic inhibition.

claim: The Na+/K+-ATPase, ion conductances, impermeant anions, electrodiffusion, water fluxes and cation-chloride cotransporters (CCCs) play roles in setting the Cl- driving force.
source: Using numerical and novel analytic solutions, we demonstrate that the Na+/K+-ATPase, ion conductances, impermeant anions, electrodiffusion, water fluxes and cation-chloride cotransporters (CCCs) play roles in setting the Cl- driving force.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Impermeant anions can contribute to setting [Cl-]i in neurons.
source: Our models, together with experimental validation, show that while impermeant anions can contribute to setting [Cl-]i in neurons, they have a negligible effect on the driving force for Cl- locally and cell-wide.
evidence: This is supported by both modeling results and experimental validation using electroporation of anionic dextrans.

claim: Impermeant anions have a negligible effect on the driving force for Cl- locally and cell-wide.
source: Our models, together with experimental validation, show that while impermeant anions can contribute to setting [Cl-]i in neurons, they have a negligible effect on the driving force for Cl- locally and cell-wide.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling and experimental validation showing that changes in impermeant anions affect both ECl and Vm similarly, resulting in negligible changes to driving force.

claim: CCCs are well-suited for modulating Cl- driving force and hence inhibitory signaling in neurons.
source: In contrast, we demonstrate that CCCs are well-suited for modulating Cl- driving force and hence inhibitory signaling in neurons.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results, furosemide experiments, and meta-analysis of literature showing correlation between KCC2 expression and driving force.

claim: Fast synaptic inhibition in the nervous system is mediated by type A γ-aminobutyric acid receptors (GABAARs) and glycine receptors (GlyRs), which are primarily permeable to chloride (Cl-).
source: Fast synaptic inhibition in the nervous system is mediated by type A γ-aminobutyric acid receptors (GABAARs) and glycine receptors (GlyRs), which are primarily permeable to chloride (Cl-) (Farrant and Kaila, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The transmembrane gradient for Cl-, together with the neuronal membrane potential, sets the driving force for Cl- flux across GABAARs and GlyRs, controlling the properties of inhibitory signaling.
source: Together with the neuronal membrane potential, the transmembrane gradient for Cl- sets the driving force for Cl- flux across these receptors, controlling the properties of inhibitory signaling.
evidence: This is a fundamental biophysical principle stated in the introduction.

claim: Modification of neuronal intracellular Cl- concentration ([Cl-]i) has been shown to play a causative role in multiple neurological diseases including epilepsy, chronic pain, schizophrenia and autism.
source: Modification of neuronal intracellular Cl- concentration ([Cl-]i) has been shown to play a causative role in multiple neurological diseases including epilepsy, chronic pain, schizophrenia and autism (Rivera et al., 2004; Huberfeld et al., 2007; Price et al., 2009; Hyde et al., 2011; Tyzio et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Intracellular Cl- is thought to be modulated during brain development so that GABAergic transmission contributes optimally to the construction of neural circuits.
source: Similarly, intracellular Cl- is thought to be modulated during brain development so that GABAergic transmission contributes optimally to the construction of neural circuits (Ben-Ari, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Plasmalemmal Cl- transporters, in particular cation-chloride cotransporters (CCCs), are understood to be the major mechanism by which neurons regulate the driving force for Cl- permeable anion channels.
source: Plasmalemmal Cl- transporters, in particular cation-chloride cotransporters (CCCs), are understood to be the major mechanism by which neurons regulate the driving force for Cl- permeable anion channels (Kaila et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: It has been suggested that impermeant anions control local [Cl-]i and driving force, rather than the CCCs.
source: Recently, it has been suggested that in fact impermeant anions control local [Cl-]i and driving force (Glykys et al., 2014), rather than the CCCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent publication that the current manuscript aims to address.

claim: The majority of intracellular anions are impermeant to the neuronal membrane; these include ribo- and deoxynucleotides, intracellular proteins and metabolites.
source: The majority of intracellular anions are impermeant to the neuronal membrane; these include ribo- and deoxynucleotides, intracellular proteins and metabolites (Burton, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Impermeant anions induce what is known as the Donnan (or Gibbs-Donnan) effect – an uneven distribution of impermeant molecules across the membrane which is osmotically unstable.
source: Impermeant anions induce what is known as the Donnan (or Gibbs-Donnan) effect (Hill, 1956; Sperelakis, 2012) – an uneven distribution of impermeant molecules across the membrane which is osmotically unstable.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established biophysical literature.

claim: Without active ion transport to counter the Donnan effect, neurons would swell and burst.
source: Without active ion transport to counter this effect, neurons would swell and burst (Kay, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Animal cells, including neurons, maintain cell volume in the presence of impermeant anions by using the Na+/K+-ATPase to pump Na+ out of the cell and K+ in, along with the passive movement of water and other ions.
source: Animal cells, including neurons, maintain cell volume in the presence of impermeant anions by using the Na+/K+-ATPase to pump Na+ out of the cell and K+ in, along with the passive movement of water and other ions (Tosteson and Hoffman, 1960; Armstrong, 2003; Liang et al., 2007; Kay, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The pump-leak mechanism, whilst stabilizing cell volume, also establishes the negative resting membrane potential and transmembrane Na+ and K+ gradients, which serve as energy sources for the coupled transport of other molecules, including Cl- by CCCs.
source: This pump-leak mechanism, whilst stabilizing cell volume, also establishes the negative resting membrane potential and transmembrane Na+ and K+ gradients, which serve as energy sources for the coupled transport of other molecules, including Cl- by CCCs.
evidence: This is a statement of established biophysical principles.

claim: The model converged to stable fixed points without needing to include any means for 'sensing' ion concentration, volume or voltage, regardless of initial starting concentrations of permeant or impermeant ions, cell volume or Vm.
source: Importantly, regardless of initial starting concentrations of permeant or impermeant ions, cell volume or Vm, the model converged to stable fixed points without needing to include any means for 'sensing' ion concentration, volume or voltage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Initial permeable ion concentrations did not influence the final cellular volume.
source: Initial permeable ion concentrations also did not influence the final cellular volume.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Despite initiating the model with different starting concentrations of Cl- (1, 15, 40 and 60 mM), [Cl-]i always converged to the same stable concentration of 5.2 mM.
source: For example, despite initiating the model with different starting concentrations of Cl- (1, 15, 40 and 60 mM, respectively, Figure 1B), [Cl-]i always converged to the same stable concentration of 5.2 mM, a typical baseline [Cl-]i for adult neurons, and volume always converged to 2.0 pL, a typical volume for hippocampal neurons (Ambros-Ingerson and Holmes, 2005).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1B and supported by a citation for typical neuronal values.

claim: Volume always converged to 2.0 pL, a typical volume for hippocampal neurons.
source: For example, despite initiating the model with different starting concentrations of Cl- (1, 15, 40 and 60 mM, respectively, Figure 1B), [Cl-]i always converged to the same stable concentration of 5.2 mM, a typical baseline [Cl-]i for adult neurons, and volume always converged to 2.0 pL, a typical volume for hippocampal neurons (Ambros-Ingerson and Holmes, 2005).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1B and supported by a citation for typical neuronal values.

claim: The model's convergence to a stable steady state does not depend on a narrow set of parameters and initial values.
source: The model is robust in the sense that its convergence to a stable steady state does not depend on a narrow set of parameters and initial values.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results showing convergence from different initial conditions.

claim: Trying an alternative model of the Na+/K+-ATPase produced similar results.
source: Trying an alternative model of the Na+/K+-ATPase (Hamada et al., 2003) produced similar results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: 'Turning off' the activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase in the model led to a progressive collapse of transmembrane ion gradients, progressive membrane depolarization and continuous and unstable cell swelling.
source: Consistent with previous results (Xiao et al., 2002; Dierkes et al., 2006; Dijkstra et al., 2016), 'turning off' the activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase in our model led to a progressive collapse of transmembrane ion gradients, progressive membrane depolarization and continuous and unstable cell swelling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with previous research.

claim: The effects of turning off the Na+/K+-ATPase could be reversed by reactivation of the pump.
source: Such effects could be reversed by reactivation of the pump (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The relative activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase sets the final stable values for ion concentrations (of both permeable and impermeant ions), Vm and volume.
source: The relative activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase sets the final stable values for ion concentrations (of both permeable and impermeant ions), Vm and volume (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: When the activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase was increased in the model, the final steady-state concentration for K+ increased, whilst Na+ and Cl- dropped to levels that approximate those observed in mature neurons.
source: When we increased the activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase in our model, the final steady-state concentration for K+ increased, whilst Na+ and Cl- dropped to levels that approximate those observed in mature neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Beyond a certain level, further increases in Na+/K+-ATPase activity have negligible effects on cell volume and transmembrane voltage.
source: Interestingly, as has been observed previously (Fraser and Huang, 2004), beyond a certain level, further increases in Na+/K+-ATPase activity have negligible effects on cell volume and transmembrane voltage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1D and is consistent with previous research.

claim: Although sufficient Na+/K+-ATPase activity is critical for steady state ionic gradients including that of Cl-, these are relatively stable near the default pump rate.
source: Note that although sufficient Na+/K+-ATPase activity is critical for steady state ionic gradients including that of Cl-, these are relatively stable near the default pump rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exact correspondence was observed between the numerical and analytic solutions within the model.
source: We observed exact correspondence between the numerical and analytic solutions within our model (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Increasing the baseline K+ conductance (gK) resulted in ECl, EK and Vm converging to similar steady-state values without significantly affecting cell volume.
source: Increasing the baseline K+ conductance (gK) resulted in ECl, EK and Vm converging to similar steady-state values (Figure 2A) without significantly affecting cell volume.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The model was able to replicate the classic dependence of membrane potential on log([K+]o).
source: We were also able to replicate the classic dependence of membrane potential on log([K+]o) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing the baseline Na+ conductance (gNa) beyond 20 µS/cm2 resulted in a steady increase of ECl, Vm and volume with a minimal increase of EK.
source: In contrast, increasing the baseline Na+ conductance (gNa) beyond 20 µS/cm2 resulted in a steady increase of ECl, Vm and volume with a minimal increase of EK (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EK is maintained in the face of increased passive K+ efflux accompanying membrane depolarization due to increased active influx of K+ by the Na+-dependent ATPase which increases its effective pump rate due to increased intracellular Na+ concentration with larger gNa.
source: EK is maintained in the face of increased passive K+ efflux accompanying membrane depolarization due to increased active influx of K+ by the Na+-dependent ATPase which increases its effective pump rate due to increased intracellular Na+ concentration with larger gNa (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the presence of active cation-chloride cotransport (gKCC2 = 20 µS/cm2), increasing Cl- conductance shifted steady state ECl from EK toward Vm.
source: In the presence of active cation-chloride cotransport (gKCC2 = 20 µS/cm2), increasing Cl- conductance shifted steady state ECl from EK toward Vm.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the absence of KCC2 activity, gCl had no effect on steady state parameters, and ECl equals Vm in all instances.
source: In the absence of KCC2 activity, gCl had no effect on steady state parameters. ECl equals Vm in all instances.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At very low values of gCl in the presence of active KCC2, the steady state [Cl-]i is such that ECl approaches EK.
source: In the presence of active KCC2 at very low values of gCl, the steady state [Cl-]i is such that ECl approaches EK.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the absence of alternative Cl- fluxes, KCC2 utilizes the transmembrane K+ gradient to transport Cl- until ECl equals EK.
source: This follows because in the absence of alternative Cl- fluxes, KCC2 utilizes the transmembrane K+ gradient to transport Cl- until ECl equals EK.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biophysical properties of KCC2.

claim: Without the activity of KCC2, any non-zero gCl had no effect on steady state ECl, EK, Vm or volume, and ECl always equals Vm.
source: Without the activity of KCC2, any non-zero gCl had no effect on steady state ECl, EK, Vm or volume (Figure 2D). In this instance ECl always equals Vm as the movement of Cl- across the membrane is purely passive.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Without the activity of KCC2, there can be no driving force for Cl- flux at steady state (Vm-ECl = 0).
source: Without the activity of KCC2, there can be no driving force for Cl- flux at steady state (Vm-ECl = 0).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The model behaved in a manner consistent with established theoretical predictions.
source: Our model therefore behaved in a manner consistent with established theoretical predictions (Kaila et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing the model results to established theory.

claim: Increasing KCC2 activity over time caused a steady decrease in [Cl-]i reflected by a hyperpolarization of ECl.
source: Increasing KCC2 activity over time caused a steady decrease in [Cl-]i reflected by a hyperpolarization of ECl (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Increasing KCC2 activity resulted in only a modest decrease in Vm, resulting in an increase in the driving force for Cl- flux that tracks the increase in gKCC2.
source: Vm decreased only modestly, resulting in an increase in the driving force for Cl- flux that tracks the increase in gKCC2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The effect of increasing KCC2 activity on driving force saturates as EK constitutes a lower bound on ECl.
source: This effect saturates as EK constitutes a lower bound on ECl.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Increases in gKCC2 resulted in persistent changes to ECl and the driving force for Cl-.
source: Importantly, increases in gKCC2 resulted in persistent changes to ECl and the driving force for Cl-.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Employing alternate models for KCC2 and the Na+/K+-ATPase did not change the result that KCC2 activity affects driving force when compensation for parameterization was given.
source: Employing alternate models for KCC2 (Fraser and Huang, 2004; Lewin et al., 2012; Raimondo et al., 2012) and the Na+/K+-ATPase (Hamada et al., 2003) did not change this result when compensation for parameterization was given, although different KCC2 models result in different kinetic rates for Cl- and K+ transport (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: With no KCC2 activity (gKCC2 = 0), ECl equaled Vm and the Cl- driving force was zero.
source: In confirmation of our findings in Figure 2D, with no KCC2 activity (gKCC2 = 0), ECl equaled Vm and the Cl- driving force was zero.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: As gKCC2 was increased, steady state ECl pulled away from Vm and approached EK, resulting in an increase in Cl- driving force (Vm-ECl).
source: As we increased gKCC2, steady state ECl pulled away from Vm and approached EK. This resulted in an increase in Cl- driving force (Vm-ECl) with steady state values of 11.3 mV at our chosen default value of gKCC2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After furosemide was introduced, EGABA became significantly more depolarized (baseline: −78.8 ± 2.8 mV vs furosemide: −71.6 ± 3.0 mV, n = 10, p=0.01, paired t-test).
source: We noted that after furosemide was introduced the EGABA became significantly more depolarized (baseline: −78.8 ± 2.8 mV vs furosemide: −71.6 ± 3.0 mV, n = 10, p=0.01, paired t-test), whilst there was no significant difference in Vm (−69.9 ± 1.8 mV vs −71.5 ± 2.6 mV, n = 10, p=0.36, paired t-test) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is experimental data from gramicidin perforated patch-clamp recordings.

claim: After furosemide was introduced, there was no significant difference in Vm (−69.9 ± 1.8 mV vs −71.5 ± 2.6 mV, n = 10, p=0.36, paired t-test).
source: We noted that after furosemide was introduced the EGABA became significantly more depolarized (baseline: −78.8 ± 2.8 mV vs furosemide: −71.6 ± 3.0 mV, n = 10, p=0.01, paired t-test), whilst there was no significant difference in Vm (−69.9 ± 1.8 mV vs −71.5 ± 2.6 mV, n = 10, p=0.36, paired t-test) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is experimental data from gramicidin perforated patch-clamp recordings.

claim: Furosemide application resulted in a significant change in the GABAAR driving force (8.9 ± 3.4 mV vs 0.1 ± 4.6 mV, n = 10, p=0.04, paired t-test).
source: This reflects a significant change in the GABAAR driving force (8.9 ± 3.4 mV vs 0.1 ± 4.6 mV, n = 10, p=0.04, paired t-test).
evidence: This is experimental data from gramicidin perforated patch-clamp recordings.

claim: The change in driving force after furosemide application persisted for at least 15 min post-application.
source: We then noted that this change in driving force persisted for at least 15 min post-application of furosemide (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is experimental data from gramicidin perforated patch-clamp recordings.

claim: A meta-analysis of seven studies and eight experiments showed a significant correlation (R2 = 0.796, p<0.001) between the change in KCC2 expression and Cl- driving force.
source: Indeed, in a meta-analysis of seven studies and eight experiments from our review of 26 studies, weighted for methodological biases and data quality, we observed a significant correlation (R2 = 0.796, p<0.001) between the change in KCC2 expression and Cl- driving force (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a meta-analysis of experimental data from the literature.

claim: Absolute changes in Vm were less than 2 mV in all but one study in the meta-analysis, meaning that the change in driving force could be ascribed to significant shifts in EGABA (R2 = 0.045, p<0.001).
source: Absolute changes in Vm were less than 2 mV in all but one study, meaning that the change in driving force could be ascribed to significant shifts in EGABA (R2 = 0.045, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a meta-analysis of experimental data from the literature.

claim: The meta-analysis supports the prediction that cation-chloride cotransport by KCC2 is an important determinant of [Cl-]i (R2 = 0.83, p<0.001, nine studies) and driving force.
source: The meta-analysis supports the prediction that cation-chloride cotransport by KCC2 is an important determinant of [Cl-]i (R2 = 0.83, p<0.001, nine studies) and driving force (see Supplementary file 2 Table S2-1 for raw data, and the scoring table for weighting in Table S2-2).
evidence: This is a meta-analysis of experimental data from the literature.

claim: Regardless of the initial concentration of impermeant anions with the same mean charge (z = −0.85), over a period of minutes, the cell adjusted its volume to give an identical steady-state impermeant anion concentration ([A]i = 155 mM).
source: We initiated the full single-compartment model with different starting concentrations of impermeant anions all with the same mean charge, z = −0.85, and observed that regardless of the initial concentration of impermeant anions, over a period of minutes, the cell adjusted its volume to give an identical steady-state impermeant anion concentration (Figure 4A, [A]i = 155 mM).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Analytically, it can be shown that the number of moles of X determines completely the volume of the compartment, while the permeant ions alone cannot be used to predict steady state volume.
source: Analytically, it can be shown that the number of moles of X determines completely the volume of the compartment, while the permeant ions alone cannot be used to predict steady state volume (Kay, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: All initial impermeant anion concentrations resulted in identical steady state values of ECl (−83.8 mV), EK (−95.1 mV) and Vm (−72.6 mV).
source: Similarly, all initial impermeant anion concentrations resulted in identical steady state values of ECl (−83.8 mV), EK (−95.1 mV) and Vm (−72.6 mV) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Simply adjusting the amount of impermeant anions within a cell has no persistent effect on [Cl-]i.
source: This shows that simply adjusting the amount of impermeant anions within a cell has no persistent effect on [Cl-]i.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Addition of impermeant anions of the mean charge (z = −0.85) caused transient shifts in ECl, EK, Vm as well as [X]i for the duration of the influx, and sustained increases in volume, but no persistent changes in ECl, EK or Vm were observed.
source: Addition of impermeant anions of the mean charge (z = −0.85) caused transients shifts in ECl (green, top panel), EK (purple), Vm (black) as well as [X]i (orange, bottom panel) for the duration of the influx, and sustained increases in volume (black, middle panel). No persistent changes in ECl, EK or Vm were observed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The inward flux of impermeant anions causes fluxes of all other ions.
source: The full time-dependent ionic and water fluxes for the experiment are shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, which shows that the inward flux of impermeant anions causes fluxes of all other ions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of extracellular impermeant anions in an osmoneutral manner causes transient shifts in the permeable ion gradients, and sustained changes in cellular volume as well as the extracellular X and extracellular and intracellular Cl- concentrations.
source: Similarly, the addition of extracellular impermeant anions in an osmoneutral manner causes transient shifts in the permeable ion gradients (top panel, colours as in 'C'), and sustained changes in cellular volume (black, middle panel) as well as the extracellular X and extracellular and intracellular Cl- concentrations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There are transient transmembrane fluxes of all ions while anions are added into the cell, and in particular the inward flux of the cations Na+ and K+, such that the sum [X]i + [Cl-]i is not necessarily kept constant during impermeant anion addition.
source: There are transient transmembrane fluxes of all ions while anions are added into the cell, and in particular the inward flux of the cations Na+ and K+, such that the sum [X]i + [Cl-]i is not necessarily kept constant during impermeant anion addition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Additions of impermeant ions in the extracellular space resulted in a temporary depolarization of ECl and Vm, but no persistent shift in these parameters.
source: Additions in the extracellular space, similarly, resulted in a temporary depolarization of ECl and Vm, but no persistent shift in these parameters (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The addition of extracellular impermeant anions resulted in a small compensatory decrease in cell volume secondary to the large shifts in [Cl-]i required to maintain the proportion of [Cl-]i to [Cl-]o according to the Nernst potential.
source: The addition of extracellular impermeant anions did however result in a small compensatory decrease in cell volume secondary to the large shifts in [Cl-]i required to maintain the proportion of [Cl-]i to [Cl-]o according to the Nernst potential.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is no lasting effect on the reversal potential or driving force for Cl- if only the concentration of a neuron's intracellular or extracellular impermeant anions is altered.
source: In summary, there is no lasting effect on the reversal potential or driving force for Cl- if only the concentration of a neuron's intracellular or extracellular impermeant anions is altered.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Concentration changes of impermeant anions alone modulate only osmoneutrality, whereas changes to intracellular charge balance affect electroneutrality and therefore the membrane and ionic potentials.
source: This is because concentration changes alone modulate only osmoneutrality, whereas changes to intracellular charge balance affect electroneutrality and therefore the membrane and ionic potentials, which we tested next.
evidence: This is an inference based on biophysical principles.

claim: Decreasing the mean charge of impermeant anions from −0.85 to −1 resulted in both a transient and persistent decrease in ECl, EK and Vm.
source: We modified the mean charge (z) of intracellular impermeant anions from −0.85 to −1 whilst measuring accompanying changes in ECl, EK, Vm and cell (Figure 5A). We found that this shift to a more negative z resulted in both a transient and persistent decrease in ECl, EK and V.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The shifts in ECl caused by changing the mean charge of impermeant anions were accompanied by broadly matching shifts in EK and Vm, which resulted in a small change in the driving force for Cl- of <0.2 mV.
source: Importantly, the shifts in ECl were accompanied by broadly matching shifts in EK and V, which resulted in a small change in the driving force for Cl- of <0.2 mV.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Changing the mean charge of impermeant anions, while substantially affecting ECl, had very small effects on the driving force for Cl-.
source: Both numerical and analytic calculation of steady state values for ECl, EK and Vm in our model showed that changing the mean charge of impermeant anions, while substantially affecting ECl, had very small effects on the driving force for Cl- (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: By shifting z within reasonable ranges for mammalian neurons, and assuming osmo- and electro-neutrality, only shifts of <1 mV in driving force could be generated.
source: By shifting z within reasonable ranges for mammalian neurons (Lodish et al., 2009; Raimondo et al., 2015), and assuming osmo- and electro-neutrality, only shifts of <1 mV could be generated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 5B and supported by citations for typical neuronal values.

claim: Although the absolute number of impermeant anions (moles) remained constant throughout the process of modifying z, cell volume shifted, and as a consequence modest alterations to the concentration of impermeant anions occurred as well.
source: In addition, although the absolute number of impermeant anions (moles) remained constant throughout the process of modifying z, cell volume shifted, and as a consequence modest alterations to the concentration of impermeant anions occurred as well.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Influx of a species of impermeant anions with a charge of −1.5, that decreased the mean charge z from −0.85 to −1 and increased the number of impermeant anions, caused persistent decreases of ECl, EK and Vm, but with larger increases in cell volume, and very small persistent changes in Cl- driving force.
source: Influx of a species of impermeant anions with a charge of −1.5, that decreased the mean charge z (bottom panel) from −0.85 to −1 and increased the number of impermeant anions also caused persistent decreases of ECl, EK and Vm as in 'A', but with larger increases in cell volume (middle panel). Again, very small persistent changes in Cl- DF were observed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Whilst large additions of impermeant anions could substantially alter the Cl- reversal potential, this had a negligible effect on the driving force for Cl- due to matching shifts in Vm.
source: Again, whilst the large additions of impermeant anions could substantially alter the Cl- reversal potential, this had a negligible effect on the driving force for Cl- due to matching shifts in Vm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Driving shifts in ECl by adding impermeant anions resulted in changes to cell volume.
source: Driving shifts in ECl in this manner also resulted in changes to cell volume (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changing the mean charge of impermeant anions, following the addition of highly negatively charged dextrans to the cell, resulted in a stable, mean negative shift in Vm from a baseline of −67.0 ± 4.0 mV to −74.0 ± 3.1 mV (n = 6, p=0.03, Wilcoxon test).
source: Once this acute perturbation had settled, as predicted by our model, changing the mean charge of impermeant anions, following the addition of highly negatively charged dextrans to the cell, resulted in a stable, mean negative shift in Vm from a baseline of −67.0 ± 4.0 mV to −74.0 ± 3.1 mV (n = 6, p=0.03, Wilcoxon test, Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recordings with electroporation of anionic dextrans.

claim: Addition of impermeant anions resulted in a significant reduction of resting EGABA (a proxy for ECl) from baseline values of −72.5 ± 2.0 mV to −77.3 ± 1.4 mV (p=0.03, Wilcoxon test).
source: Again in line with our predictions, addition of impermeant anions also resulted in a significant reduction of resting EGABA (a proxy for ECl) from baseline values of −72.5 ± 2.0 mV to −77.3 ± 1.4 mV (p=0.03, Wilcoxon test).
evidence: This is experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recordings with electroporation of anionic dextrans.

claim: Similar shifts in Vm and EGABA following addition of impermeant anions resulted in an undetectable shift in GABA and hence Cl- driving force (5.5 ± 4.4 mV vs 3.3 ± 3.5 mV, n = 6, p=0.22, Wilcoxon test).
source: Importantly, however, similar shifts in Vm and EGABA resulted in an undetectable shift in GABA and hence Cl- driving force (5.5 ± 4.4 mV vs 3.3 ± 3.5 mV, n = 6, p=0.22, Wilcoxon test, Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recordings with electroporation of anionic dextrans.

claim: Whilst the adjustment of mean impermeant anion charge can significantly affect ECl, this results in negligible changes to the driving force for Cl-.
source: Our single-compartment model of Cl- homeostasis, in conjunction with experimental validation, demonstrates that whilst the adjustment of mean impermeant anion charge can significantly affect ECl, this results in negligible changes to the driving force for Cl-.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from both modeling and experimental results.

claim: Adjusting the activity of cation-chloride cotransport modulates both ECl and the driving force for Cl- substantially.
source: This contrasts with the results shown earlier, where adjusting the activity of cation-chloride cotransport modulates both ECl and the driving force for Cl- substantially.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: When the Na+/K+-ATPase effective pump rate was fixed at a constant value, adjusting the mean charge of impermeant anions generated no persistent change in Cl- driving force.
source: In the case where the pump rate was fixed, adjusting the mean charge of impermeant anions generated no persistent change in Cl- driving force (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Small shifts in Cl- driving force occurred only when the effective pump rate was variable, in which minor changes to [Na+]i caused significant changes to Jp, which in turn resulted in a small shift in Cl- driving force.
source: However, small shifts in Cl- driving force occurred only when the effective pump rate was variable, in which minor changes to [Na+]i caused significant changes to Jp, which in turn resulted in a small shift in Cl- driving force.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is a direct relationship between the mean charge of impermeant anions (z), [Na+]i, the effective Na+/K+-ATPase pump rate and Cl- driving force.
source: There is a direct relationship between the mean charge of impermeant anions (z), [Na+]i, the effective Na+/K+-ATPase pump rate and Cl- driving force.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The relationship between impermeant anion charge and Cl- driving force was abolished when the effective Na+/K+-ATPase pump rate was held constant by removing its dependence on Na+.
source: This relationship was abolished when the effective Na+/K+-ATPase pump rate was held constant by removing its dependence on Na+ (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Even large variations in effective pump rate near the default value caused negligible shifts in Cl- driving force of <1 mV.
source: In addition, even large variations in effective pump rate near the default value caused negligible shifts in Cl- driving force of <1 mV.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Small, impermeant anion driven, Na+/K+-ATPase pump-dependent shifts in Cl- driving force are completely dependent on the presence of cation-chloride cotransport.
source: These small, impermeant anion driven, Na+/K+-ATPase pump-dependent shifts in Cl- driving force are completely dependent on the presence of cation-chloride cotransport.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In the absence of KCC2, there is no Cl- driving force as ECl = Vm.
source: In the absence of KCC2, there is no Cl- driving force as ECl = Vm (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Adding impermeant anions of the same charge as the mean charge of the cell with a volume constraint resulted in a small change in driving force when Jp was variable, but not when Jp was held constant.
source: Impermeant anions of the same charge as the mean charge of the cell were added. A volume constraint was incorporated by adding a hydrostatic force dependent on membrane tension (dashed lines), which resulted in an impermeable anion-induced transmembrane osmotic differential. This caused a small change in DF when Jp was variable (dashed line), but not when Jp was held constant (dotted lines).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Impermeant anion-induced cell swelling in the presence of volume constraints (i.e. membrane tension) results in steady states with equal but non-zero osmotic and hydrostatic pressures, causing transmembrane osmotic differences, which causes small changes in Na+, and hence Jp.
source: Schematic explaining the mechanism through which impermeant anion-induced cell swelling in the presence of volume constraints (i.e. membrane tension) result in steady states with equal but non-zero osmotic (osmoP) and hydrostatic pressures (HP), causing transmembrane osmotic differences (t1). This causes small changes in Na+, and hence Jp.
evidence: This is explained in the schematic in Figure 6E and demonstrated by the modeling results.

claim: All Na+/K+-ATPase pump rate-related shifts in the driving force require KCC2 activity; in the absence of activity, no shifts in driving force can occur.
source: All Na+/K+-ATPase pump rate-related shifts in the DF require KCC2 activity; in the absence of activity (dashes), no shifts in driving force can occur.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Changes in Cl- driving force generated by changing the ionic contributions to cellular charge (by altering the mean charge of impermeant anions) or osmoneutrality (by increasing the contribution of hydrostatic pressure) are due to the alteration of the dynamics of active ion transport mechanisms in the cell.
source: In summary, changes in Cl- driving force generated by changing the ionic contributions to cellular charge (by altering the mean charge of impermeant anions) or osmoneutrality (by increasing the contribution of hydrostatic pressure) are due to the alteration of the dynamics of active ion transport mechanisms in the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The effects of impermeant anions on driving force are negligible in magnitude and cannot contribute significantly to setting physiologically observed Cl- driving forces.
source: However, these effects are negligible in magnitude and cannot contribute significantly to setting physiologically observed Cl- driving forces.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Any non-zero Cl- driving force is entirely dependent on the presence of active Cl- cotransport.
source: It is worth reiterating that any non-zero Cl- driving force is entirely dependent on the presence of active Cl- cotransport.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: In the absence of KCC2, neither the Na+/K+-ATPase nor impermeable anions can shift Cl- out of equilibrium.
source: In our model, in the absence of KCC2, neither the Na+/K+-ATPase nor impermeable anions can shift Cl- out of equilibrium (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Selectively increasing the conductance of KCC2 in one compartment of the virtual dendrite resulted in a persistent decrease in ECl, concurrent with a modest decrease in Vm, resulting in a permanent increase in Cl- driving force and minimal change in compartment volume.
source: To explore the local effects of CCC activity, we increased gKCC2 from our default value of 20 µS/cm2 to 600 µS/cm2 in the second distal compartment of the virtual dendrite exclusively. This resulted in a persistent decrease in ECl, concurrent with a modest decrease in Vm, resulting in a permanent increase in Cl- driving force and minimal change in compartment volume (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The spatial precision of alterations in Cl- driving force by local KCC2 activity depended strongly on the diffusion constant for Cl-.
source: The spatial precision of this alteration depended strongly on the diffusion constant for Cl-.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: With a Cl- diffusion constant of 2.03 × 10−7 dm2.s−1, alterations in Cl- driving force spread widely through the virtual dendrite.
source: With a Cl- diffusion constant of 2.03 × 10−7 dm2.s−1, these alterations spread widely through the virtual dendrite. For example, the change in Cl- driving force was 4.8 mV in the furthermost compartment (90 μm apart) as compared to 5.9 mV in the compartment manipulated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: When the Cl- diffusion constant was decreased by one order of magnitude, the change in Cl- driving force was 7.3 mV in the compartment in which KCC2 was adjusted, but only 1.8 mV in the furthermost compartment from the site of manipulation.
source: When we decreased the Cl- diffusion constant by one order of magnitude, the change in Cl- driving force was 7.3 mV in the compartment in which KCC2 was adjusted, but only 1.8 mV in the furthermost compartment from the site of manipulation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Local differences in cation-chloride cotransport activity can drive spatially restricted differences in Cl- driving force under conditions of constrained Cl- diffusion.
source: These findings suggest that local differences in cation-chloride cotransport activity can drive spatially restricted differences in Cl- driving force under conditions of constrained Cl- diffusion; however, under conditions of typical ionic diffusion the effect of Cl- transport by KCC2 is relatively widespread.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Under conditions of typical ionic diffusion, the effect of Cl- transport by KCC2 is relatively widespread.
source: These findings suggest that local differences in cation-chloride cotransport activity can drive spatially restricted differences in Cl- driving force under conditions of constrained Cl- diffusion; however, under conditions of typical ionic diffusion the effect of Cl- transport by KCC2 is relatively widespread.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Local addition of impermeant anions of mean charge has no local effect on Cl- homeostasis but can affect the volume of the compartment concerned.
source: This suggests that local addition of impermeant anions of mean charge has no local effect on Cl- homeostasis but can affect the volume of the compartment concerned.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Local addition of impermeant anions with a more negative charge than the current mean resulted in a persistent shift in ECl and Vm specifically in the compartment manipulated, but generated a negligible, persistent change in Cl- driving force (<0.01 mV).
source: Following cessation of local impermeant anion influx, a persistent shift in ECl and Vm was observed specifically in the compartment manipulated. However, this generated a negligible, persistent change in Cl- driving force (<0.01 mV change in driving force for a compartment specific change in z from −0.85 to −0.93), only within that specific compartment of the virtual dendrite.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Local impermeant anions can adjust the Cl- reversal potential locally, but are not well-placed to cause significant, permanent shifts in the driving force for Cl-.
source: This finding suggests that local impermeant anions can adjust the Cl- reversal potential locally, but are not well-placed to cause significant, permanent shifts in the driving force for Cl-.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Electrodiffusion may further limit the degree to which local changes in impermeant ion charge can modify driving forces through alterations in active ionic transport: the resulting permanent Cl- driving force changes in the multi-compartment model are many times smaller than the shifts in the single compartment version.
source: Indeed, electrodiffusion may further limit the degree to which local changes in impermeant ion charge can modify driving forces through alterations in active ionic transport: the resulting permanent Cl- driving force changes in the multi-compartment model are many times smaller than the shifts in the single compartment version (as compared to Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by comparing the multi-compartment modeling results to the single-compartment results.

claim: The Na+/K+-ATPase, baseline K+, Na+ and Cl- conductances, mean charge of impermeant anions, water permeability and CCCs, likely all play roles in setting neuronal [Cl-]i.
source: We show that the Na+/K+-ATPase, baseline K+, Na+ and Cl- conductances, mean charge of impermeant anions, water permeability and CCCs, likely all play roles in setting neuronal [Cl-]i.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Under physiologically relevant conditions, impermeant anions do not alter the Cl- driving force significantly.
source: Our modelling and experimental data demonstrate that under physiologically relevant conditions, impermeant anions do not alter the Cl- driving force significantly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from both modeling and experimental results.

claim: The theoretical approach is based on the pump-leak formulation.
source: Our theoretical approach is based on the pump-leak formulation (Tosteson and Hoffman, 1960).
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling approach used in the manuscript.

claim: The pump-leak formulation suggests that mammalian cells maintain their volume under osmotic stress generated by impermeant anions and the Donnan effect by employing active transport of Na+ and K+ using the Na+/K+-ATPase.
source: It suggests that mammalian cells maintain their volume under osmotic stress generated by impermeant anions and the Donnan effect by employing active transport of Na+ and K+ using the Na+/K+-ATPase (Armstrong, 2003; Kay, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the pump-leak formulation supported by citations.

claim: A Donnan equilibrium, a true thermodynamic equilibrium requiring no energy to maintain it, is not possible in cells with pliant membranes like neurons.
source: A Donnan equilibrium, a true thermodynamic equilibrium requiring no energy to maintain it, is not possible in cells with pliant membranes like neurons (Sperelakis, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about biophysical principles supported by a citation.

claim: The model conforms to the pump-leak formulation: abolishing the activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase leads to cell swelling, progressive membrane depolarization and rundown of ionic gradients, including that of Cl-.
source: Our model conforms to the pump-leak formulation: abolishing the activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase leads to cell swelling, progressive membrane depolarization and rundown of ionic gradients, including that of Cl-.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Na+/K+ ATPase is a fundamental cellular parameter that stabilizes cell volume and determines all ionic gradients including that of Cl- and hence must be considered in any attempt to model ion homeostasis.
source: Therefore, the Na+/K+ ATPase is a fundamental cellular parameter that stabilizes cell volume and determines all ionic gradients including that of Cl- and hence must be considered in any attempt to model ion homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Above a certain level of Na+/K+-ATPase activity, even many fold changes in pump rate have minimal effects on volume, ECl and Vm.
source: Interestingly however, we demonstrate that above a certain level of Na+/K+-ATPase activity, even many fold changes in pump rate have minimal effects on volume, ECl and Vm.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: It seems unlikely that neurons adjust the Na+/K+-ATPase as a means for modulating Cl- driving force.
source: It therefore seems unlikely that neurons adjust the Na+/K+-ATPase as a means for modulating Cl- driving force.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results and experimental observations.

claim: The model is consistent with recent experimental results that demonstrate that increased neuronal Na+ conductance leads to progressive neuronal swelling, membrane depolarization and Cl- accumulation – the primary pathological process in cytotoxic edema.
source: Our model is consistent with recent experimental results that demonstrate that increased neuronal Na+ conductance (for example by activating NMDA receptors, or preventing closure of voltage-gated Na+ channels), leads to progressive neuronal swelling, membrane depolarization and Cl- accumulation (Rungta et al., 2015) – the primary pathological process in cytotoxic edema (Liang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement comparing the model results to experimental findings supported by citations.

claim: Tonic neuronal Cl- conductance only affects baseline [Cl-]i and driving force in the presence of CCCs.
source: We also show that tonic neuronal Cl- conductance only affects baseline [Cl-]i and driving force in the presence of CCCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Without active Cl- flux, which CCCs provide, there is no driving force for passive Cl- flux and hence no mechanism for [Cl-]i changes resulting from selective modification of a Cl- conductance.
source: Without active Cl- flux, which CCCs provide, there is no driving force for passive Cl- flux and hence no mechanism for [Cl-]i changes resulting from selective modification of a Cl- conductance.
evidence: This is an inference based on biophysical principles.

claim: The finding that tonic Cl- conductance only affects [Cl-]i in the presence of CCCs is consistent with both classic and recent experimental findings.
source: This is consistent with both classic (Misgeld et al., 1986; Thompson and Gähwiler, 1989) and recent experimental findings (Berglund et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement comparing the model results to experimental findings supported by citations.

claim: Elevating the activity of KCC2 increases the driving force for Cl- by shifting the reversal potential for Cl- closer to that of K+.
source: In our model, we find that elevating the activity of KCC2, the most active CCC in mature neurons (Ben-Ari, 2002), increases the driving force for Cl- by shifting the reversal potential for Cl- closer to that of K+.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Large shifts (~7 mV) in driving force by modulating KCC2 were associated with very minor (1%) changes in volume or membrane potential.
source: Interestingly, large shifts (~7 mV) in driving force were associated with very minor (1%) changes in volume or membrane potential.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Modulating KCC2 represents a specific means for manipulating the neuronal Cl- driving force.
source: As such, modulating KCC2 represents a specific means for manipulating the neuronal Cl- driving force.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The finding that modulating KCC2 affects Cl- driving force is consistent with traditional dogma, recent and previous experimental results as well as experimental validation using furosemide.
source: This is consistent with traditional dogma, recent and previous experimental results (Kaila et al., 2014; Klein et al., 2018) as well as our own experimental validation using furosemide to block the activity of KCC2, which drove significant changes in driving force with little effect on Vm.
evidence: This is a statement comparing the model results to experimental findings supported by citations and experimental validation.

claim: There is an ongoing debate as to whether some cotransporters, including CCCs, might also couple water transport to ion transport.
source: There is an ongoing debate as to whether some cotransporters, including CCCs, might also couple water transport to ion transport (Zeuthen, 1994; MacAulay et al., 2002; Gagnon et al., 2004; Charron et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about an ongoing debate in the field supported by citations.

claim: Even if KCC2 couples water transport to ion transport, this scenario would not alter the central importance of CCCs for setting the Cl- driving force.
source: Although we did not model the active movement of water by KCC2, this scenario would not alter the central importance of CCCs for setting the Cl- driving force.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of water transport by KCC2.

claim: Cytoplasmic Cl- diffusion rates had to be reduced substantially before local changes in Cl- driving force driven by KCC2 were observed.
source: Cytoplasmic Cl- diffusion rates had to be reduced substantially before we observed local changes in Cl- driving force driven by KCC2 (Qian and Sejnowski, 1989; Kuner and Augustine, 2000).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 7 and supported by citations.

claim: Differences in KCC2 activity might generate a gradient in Cl- driving force between large subcellular structures (i.e. dendrites versus soma).
source: Whilst differences in KCC2 activity might generate a gradient in Cl- driving force between large subcellular structures (i.e. dendrites versus soma), our modeling results call into question the idea of synapse-specific regulation of Cl- driving force within the same cellular domain (Földy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The modeling results call into question the idea of synapse-specific regulation of Cl- driving force within the same cellular domain.
source: Whilst differences in KCC2 activity might generate a gradient in Cl- driving force between large subcellular structures (i.e. dendrites versus soma), our modeling results call into question the idea of synapse-specific regulation of Cl- driving force within the same cellular domain (Földy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Glykys et al. (2014) used Cl- imaging and various experimental manipulations to claim that intracellular and extracellular concentrations of impermeant anions ([X]i and [X]o) set [Cl-]i and the Cl- driving force.
source: Glykys et al. (2014) used Cl- imaging and various experimental manipulations to claim that intracellular and extracellular concentrations of impermeant anions ([X]i and [X]o) set [Cl-]i and the Cl- driving force.
evidence: This is a statement about a previous publication that the current manuscript aims to address.

claim: From the theoretical analysis, modifying the amount of impermeant anions inside or outside neurons has no persistent effect on [Cl-]i or Cl- driving force, unless a mechanism that allows a transmembrane osmotic pressure differential to develop that indirectly affects active transport mechanisms is included.
source: From our theoretical analysis, we find that modifying the amount of impermeant anions inside or outside neurons has no persistent effect on [Cl-]i or Cl- driving force, unless we include a mechanism that allows a transmembrane osmotic pressure differential to develop that indirectly affects active transport mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown in Figure 4 and Figure 6.

claim: Even with a mechanism that allows transmembrane osmotic pressure differentials, under transmembrane pressure differentials that do not lyse the membrane, Cl- driving force changes are negligible (<1 mV).
source: Even in this case, under transmembrane pressure differentials that do not lyse the membrane (Nichol and Hutter, 1996), Cl- driving force changes are negligible (<1 mV).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6C and supported by a citation.

claim: It has been suggested that the viscoelastic properties of the cellular cytoskeleton could allow it to take up osmotic shifts created by impermeant anion movement like a sponge.
source: Recently, it has been suggested that the viscoelastic properties of the cellular cytoskeleton could allow it to take up osmotic shifts created by impermeant anion movement like a sponge (Sachs and Sivaselvan, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about a recent suggestion in the literature supported by a citation.

claim: If the cytoskeleton takes up osmotic shifts like a sponge, one would not see as large a volume shifts as predicted by the models.
source: This would mean that one would not see as large a volume shifts as predicted by our models.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the cytoskeleton acting like a sponge.

claim: Although it is thought that some neurons do not express aquaporin channels, water can permeate the phospholipid bilayer.
source: Although it is thought that some neurons do not express aquaporin channels (Andrew et al., 2007), water can permeate the phospholipid bilayer (Fettiplace and Haydon, 1980).
evidence: This is a statement about water permeability supported by citations.

claim: Whilst differences in neuronal water permeability might affect the time taken to reach steady-state, the steady state values themselves are unlikely to be affected.
source: Therefore, whilst differences in neuronal water permeability might affect the time taken to reach steady-state, the steady state values themselves are unlikely to be affected.
evidence: This is an inference based on biophysical principles.

claim: [Cl-]i and the Cl- driving force are not determined by the concentration of impermeant anions.
source: We conclude that [Cl-]i and the Cl- driving force are not determined by the concentration of impermeant anions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Modifying the mean charge of impermeant anions (i.e. z in [Xz]i), rather than their concentration, can affect [Cl-]i and ECl.
source: However, our theoretical findings offer a potential explanation for recent experimental observations. We show that modifying the mean charge of impermeant anions (i.e. z in [Xz]i), rather than their concentration, can affect [Cl-]i and ECl.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: If the manipulation by Glykys et al. (2014) using SYTO64 staining and perfusion of weak organic acids modifies the mean charge of internal impermeant anions, and not concentration per se, this could account for the observed changes in [Cl-]i.
source: Relating this to prior experimental observations, Glykys et al. (2014) used SYTO64 staining of nucleic acids and perfusion of weak organic acids in conjunction with Cl- imaging to suggest that [Cl-]i depends upon internal impermeant anions ([X]i). If such a manipulation modifies the mean charge of internal impermeant anions, and not concentration per se, this could account for the observed changes in [Cl-]i.
evidence: This is a speculation about the interpretation of previous experimental results.

claim: Glykys et al. (2014) did not measure Vm or the Cl- driving force in the experiments using SYTO64 staining and weak organic acids.
source: Glykys et al. (2014) did not measure Vm or the Cl- driving force in these experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about what was not measured in a previous publication.

claim: The clear prediction from the model is that any manipulation, which changes the mean charge of impermeant anions would not appreciably affect the Cl- driving force because any impermeant anion driven change on ECl- is matched by an equivalent effect on Vm due to accompanying shifts in cation concentrations.
source: The clear prediction from our model is that any manipulation, which changes the mean charge of impermeant anions would not appreciably affect the Cl- driving force because any impermeant anion driven change on ECl- is matched by an equivalent effect on Vm due to accompanying shifts in cation concentrations.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Experimental support for the prediction that changing impermeant anion charge does not affect driving force was provided by showing that whilst EGABA (and ECl) can be shifted by addition of impermeant anions using electroporation of membrane impermeant anionic dextrans, Vm is shifted in a similar direction resulting in an undetectable change in Cl- driving force.
source: We have provided experimental support for this prediction by showing that whilst EGABA (and ECl) can be shifted by addition of impermeant anions using electroporation of membrane impermeant anionic dextrans, Vm is shifted in a similar direction resulting in an undetectable change in Cl- driving force.
evidence: This is experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recordings with electroporation of anionic dextrans shown in Figure 5.

claim: Future experiments could further test the model by electroporating positively charged dextrans which would be predicted to depolarize both Vm and ECl, again with minimal effects on Cl- driving force.
source: Future experiments could further test our model by electroporating positively charged dextrans which would be predicted to depolarize both Vm and ECl, again with minimal effects on Cl- driving force.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experiments based on the model predictions.

claim: Given prior theoretical predictions, it is interesting that the model reveals that changing impermeant anions could affect the Cl- driving force at all.
source: Given prior theoretical predictions (Kaila et al., 2014; Voipio et al., 2014; Savtchenko et al., 2017), it is interesting that our model reveals that changing impermeant anions could affect the Cl- driving force at all.
evidence: This is a statement comparing the model results to prior theoretical predictions supported by citations.

claim: The small (<1 mV) impermeant anion-driven changes in Cl- driving force observed in the model were caused by indirect effects on Na+ concentration and hence Na+/K+-ATPase activity.
source: We found that the small (<1 mV) impermeant anion-driven changes in Cl- driving force observed in our model were caused by indirect effects on Na+ concentration and hence Na+/K+-ATPase activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The impermeant anion-driven changes in Cl- driving force are even smaller in the multi-compartment model (<0.1 mV), in which electrodiffusion allows local changes in Na+ to dissipate.
source: The impermeant anion-driven changes in Cl- driving force are even smaller in the multi-compartment model (<0.1 mV), in which electrodiffusion allows local changes in Na+ to dissipate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the multi-compartment modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: When Na+/K+-ATPase activity was decoupled from the transmembrane Na+ gradient, impermeant anions were unable to cause persistent shifts in Cl- driving force as predicted theoretically.
source: When Na+/K+-ATPase activity was decoupled from the transmembrane Na+ gradient, we found that impermeant anions were unable to cause persistent shifts in Cl- driving force as predicted theoretically (Kaila et al., 2014; Voipio et al., 2014; Savtchenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6 and is consistent with prior theoretical predictions.

claim: The small, impermeant anion-Na+/K+-ATPase-driven shifts in Cl- driving force are dependent on the presence of cation-chloride cotransport in the form of KCC2 and would entail changes in energy use by the Na+/K+-ATPase.
source: It is important to note that these small, impermeant anion-Na+/K+-ATPase-driven shifts in Cl- driving force are dependent on the presence of cation-chloride cotransport in the form of KCC2 and would entail changes in energy use by the Na+/K+-ATPase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Active transport mechanisms are required to drive changes in Cl- homeostasis.
source: In other words, active transport mechanisms are again required to drive changes in Cl- homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: The theoretical models, which are derived from well-established physical principles, are consistent with experimental data and suggest that impermeant anions alone cannot shift Cl- out of equilibrium across the neuronal membrane.
source: In summary, our theoretical models, which are derived from well-established physical principles, are consistent with our own experimental data and that of others (Glykys et al., 2014; Kaila et al., 2014; Klein et al., 2018), and suggest that impermeant anions alone cannot shift Cl- out of equilibrium across the neuronal membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from both modeling and experimental results.

claim: Were neurons to alter impermeant anion concentration or charge, the resting membrane potential would be modified with little effect on the Cl- driving force.
